rationale: A wins because it finds the hard story, not just the launch wrapper: "Replit says anyone can build an app with plain English. It won't say how often those apps actually work." B has discipline, but its money angle overreaches with "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" from a thin pricing fact, and it never promotes the undisclosed reliability number into a real angle. A has one speculative security reach, but its best angles are reporter-ready questions with the proof gaps named in plain daylight.
gaps_in_A: "huge, largely non-technical user base" is not supplied. The update says Replit is used heavily in education and positions this agent for non-engineers; it does not prove the existing user base is largely non-technical.

"Replit's new agent lets non-coders spin up live databases. Who's checking what's in them?" is a strong question, but it edges toward implied security risk without evidence of exposed data, organizational use, or real misconfiguration.

"Replit's usage-based pricing shows where AI agent costs are headed" gets refused as `duplicate`; wrong diagnosis. Pricing is a distinct money lens, just too thin without tiers, examples, or cost comparisons.

"turn its tens of millions of users into app publishers overnight" leans hard on a company-claimed count and implies immediate publishing behavior by all users. It needs active-user definition before that headline can carry weight.
gaps_in_B: "When the AI does the building, Replit charges for the work, not the seat" overstates the supplied fact. Usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions is not proof that Replit is charging for work instead of seats.
B buries the strongest accountability angle as proof: "how often generated apps work without fixes" should be its own story, not a footnote under the category pitch.

"Replit bets its next users will never write a line of code" is cleaner than it is true. The update says Replit positions the agent for non-engineers and vibe coders, not that its whole next-user strategy is people who will never code.
B misses the database/security consequence entirely, even though "sets up a database" is one of the few concrete product facts that opens a different beat.
